newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament eases abortion in final vote.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament eases abortion in final vote.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Thursday overthrew a Senate veto and passed a bill liberalising abortion, despite fervent opposition from the Catholic Church and Polish-born Pope John Paul.
Deputies voted by 228 to 195 with 16 abstentions in favour of the bill, which ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski has promised to sign promptly into law.

Women will now be able to end pregnancies before the 12th week if they face financial or personal problems, after counselling and a period of reflection. The bill also calls for sex education in schools and cheaper contraception.

Under the existing anti-abortion law, passed in 1993 by a pro-Catholic government, terminations are permitted only if a pregnancy threatens a woman's life or health, results from incest or rape, or when the foetus is hopelessly damaged.
"The situation is very grim -- that parliament reacted this way," Catholic priest Marian Subocz, deputy secretary general of the Episcopate, told Reuters immediately after the vote.
The reform, first passed by the lower house in August, was blocked by the Senate this month. Its advocates needed 50 percent plus one of the votes to overturn the upper house veto.
The Church organised a huge protest campaign against the bill, culminating in a silent march on parliament on Wednesday by more than 30,000 people from around Poland.
The Pontiff said he was personally pained by the bill and last month warned his compatriots: "A nation which kills its own children is a nation without a future."
The reform was backed by the main ruling coalition party, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and some liberal or left-leaning opposition deputies.
Its supporters argued that abortion is already widely available in underground clinics or abroad to women with money.
They said the education and contraception measures would actually lessen demand for abortions and the bill would avert tragedies such as bungled terminations or abandoned infants.
"Women cannot be made to give birth under compulsion. Love cannot be accompanied by fear," SLD deputy Izabella Sierakowska told parliament during a heated debate on Wednesday.
The issue deeply split the nation and the ruling coalition.
The vast majority of the SLD's smaller, often uneasy coalition partner, the Peasant party, sided with right-leaning pro-Catholic opposition groups in opposing the bill.

The Peasants' stance helps them keep open the option of an alliance with parties grouped around the pro-Church Solidarity union -- now running about level with the SLD in opinion polls -- after parliamentary elections due in September 1997.

Opinion polls suggest that anti-abortion sentiment has been rising and that Poles, about 90 percent of whom are at least nominally Catholic, are now almost equally divided on the question, with a small majority in favour of liberal laws.
Solidarity has stood by the Church, which championed the union's pre-1989 struggle against communist rule, and may try to reverse the new abortion law if it wins next year's polls.

Former Solidarity leader Lech Walesa, who lost the Polish presidency to Aleksander Kwasniewski in elections last year, in 1994 vetoed a previous parliamentary bill to ease restrictions on abortion when he was president.
